title: Diodes
description: The pn-junction diode: forward and reverse bias, the I–V characteristic and the Shockley equation.

study.title: Terminals and references
study.body: A diode has two terminals: the **anode** (triangle side) and the **cathode** (bar side). The voltage $v_D$ is referenced + at the anode and the current $i_D$ is referenced from anode to cathode through the diode. The diode behaves like a one-way valve: it conducts easily when $v_D$ is positive and blocks when $v_D$ is negative.

study.title: The pn junction (in brief)
study.body:
A diode is a junction of **p-type** silicon (holes are the main carriers) and **n-type** silicon (free electrons are the main carriers). A potential barrier forms at the junction.
- **Forward bias** (p-side positive) lowers the barrier: a large current flows.
- **Reverse bias** (n-side positive) raises the barrier: almost no current flows.
The anode is the p-side, the cathode the n-side.

study.title: The I–V characteristic
study.body:
- **Forward bias:** hardly any current until $v_D \approx 0.6$ V, then $i_D$ rises very steeply. At typical currents a small silicon diode drops 0.6–0.7 V.
- **Reverse bias:** a tiny current $i_D \approx -I_s$ (nanoamperes or less).
- **Reverse breakdown:** at $v_D \approx -V_{BR}$ a large reverse current flows. This is not destructive as long as the power dissipation is limited; zener diodes are designed to work here.

study.title: The Shockley equation
study.body: $I_s$ is the saturation current (around $10^{-14}$ A for a small silicon diode), $n$ is the emission coefficient (between 1 and 2) and $V_T = kT/q$ is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV at 300 K. When $v_D$ is more than a few times $nV_T$, the −1 can be dropped. When $v_D$ is more negative than a few times $-nV_T$ (but not in breakdown), $i_D \approx -I_s$.

study.title: Solving for the voltage
study.body:
When the current is known, solve the Shockley equation for $v_D$. Each tenfold increase of current raises $v_D$ by $nV_T\ln 10$, about 60 mV for $n = 1$.
**Example:** $I_s = 10^{-14}$ A, $n = 1$, $i_D = 1$ mA gives $v_D = 0.026\ln(10^{11}) \approx 0.66$ V.

study.title: Temperature and pitfalls
study.body:
$V_T = kT/q$ with $k = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K and $q = 1.60\times10^{-19}$ C, so it grows with temperature. At a fixed current, the forward voltage **drops by about 2 mV per kelvin**.
- Use $V_T$ = 0.026 V (not 26) inside the exponent.
- Don't forget $n$ in $nV_T$.
- A reverse-biased diode (not in breakdown) carries $-I_s$: practically zero, but negative.

steps.title: A one-way valve for current
steps.body: A diode lets current flow easily from **anode** to **cathode** and (almost) blocks it the other way. We reference $v_D$ positive at the anode and $i_D$ flowing into the anode.

steps.prompt: For a diode to be **forward biased**, which must hold?
options: The anode is more positive than the cathode
The cathode is more positive than the anode
Anode and cathode are at the same potential
steps.explanation: Forward bias means $v_D > 0$, with $v_D$ referenced + at the anode. The barrier at the junction is lowered and $i_D$ flows from anode to cathode.

steps.title: Inside: the pn junction
steps.body:
The diode is made of **p-type** material (anode side, holes) joined to **n-type** material (cathode side, free electrons). A barrier at the junction holds the carriers back.
- Positive on the p-side lowers the barrier: large current.
- Positive on the n-side raises the barrier: almost no current.

steps.prompt: The anode of a diode is its n-type side.
steps.explanation: The anode is the **p-side** and the cathode is the **n-side**. Forward bias therefore means making the p-side (anode) positive.

steps.title: Three regions
steps.body:
- **Forward bias:** for $v_D$ above about 0.6 V the current grows very fast; a silicon diode at a few mA shows about 0.7 V.
- **Reverse bias:** only a tiny current $i_D \approx -I_s$ flows.
- **Reverse breakdown:** when $v_D$ reaches $-V_{BR}$, a large reverse current flows.

steps.prompt: Match each region of the diode characteristic with its behaviour
steps.explanation: In forward bias the current rises steeply above about 0.6 V. In reverse bias only the tiny saturation current flows (negative, because it flows from cathode to anode). At the breakdown voltage the reverse current becomes large while $v_D$ stays near $-V_{BR}$.

steps.prompt: In this circuit the diode has a breakdown voltage of 50 V. What is its state?
steps.explanation: The diode's anode is at the bottom (connected to the − terminal) and its cathode at the top (connected through R to the + terminal). The cathode is positive, so the diode is reverse biased. Only $-I_s$ flows, so the drop across R is practically zero and the whole 5 V appears across the diode: $v_D \approx -5$ V. Since 5 V is far below the 50 V breakdown voltage, there is no breakdown.

steps.prompt: Ideal diodes, $V_s$ = 5 V. Tap every diode that **conducts**.
steps.hint: Follow each branch from the + rail to the − rail. One diode pointing the wrong way blocks the whole branch.
steps.explanation:
Current can only flow through a diode from anode to cathode, in the direction of the triangle. The top rail is the + side, so a branch conducts only if **every** diode in it points down.
- $D_1$ points down: it conducts.
- $D_2$ points up, against the source: reverse biased, so its whole branch (with $R_2$) is off.
- $D_3$ and $D_4$ are back to back: $D_4$ blocks, so no current flows and $D_3$ cannot conduct either.
- $D_5$ and $D_6$ both point down: they conduct together, and $R_3$ limits the current.

steps.prompt: Operating a diode in reverse breakdown always destroys it.
steps.explanation: Breakdown is not destructive as long as the current, and therefore the power $|v_D i_D|$, is limited so the diode does not overheat. Zener diodes are made to operate in breakdown on purpose.

steps.prompt: Roughly what forward voltage does a small silicon diode show when it conducts a few milliamperes?
steps.explanation: The forward characteristic is very steep above about 0.6 V, so at typical currents $v_D$ is 0.6–0.7 V. 26 mV is the thermal voltage $V_T$, not the diode drop.

steps.title: The Shockley equation
steps.body: The diode current depends exponentially on the voltage. Use $V_T$ = 0.026 V at 300 K. For $v_D \gg nV_T$ the −1 is negligible, so $i_D \approx I_s e^{v_D/nV_T}$.

steps.prompt: A diode has $I_s = {{a}}\times10^{-14}$ A and $n = 1$. With $V_T$ = 26 mV, find $i_D$ at $v_D$ = {{vD|V}}.
steps.explanation:
$i_D = I_s\left[\exp(v_D/nV_T) - 1\right] = {{a}}\times10^{-14}\left[\exp({{vD}}/0.026) - 1\right]$ = {{iD|A}}.
The exponent is {{vD/0.026}}, so the −1 makes no visible difference.

steps.prompt: A diode with $I_s = {{a}}\times10^{-14}$ A and $n = 1$ carries $i_D$ = {{iD|A}} at 300 K ($V_T$ = 26 mV). Find $v_D$.
steps.explanation:
Solve the Shockley equation for the voltage:
$v_D = nV_T\ln\left(\frac{i_D}{I_s} + 1\right) = 0.026\ln\left(\frac{ {{iD}} }{ {{a}}\times10^{-14} } + 1\right)$ = {{vD|V}}.

steps.prompt: A diode with $n$ = {{n}} is well into forward conduction at 300 K. Its voltage $v_D$ is raised by {{dV|V}}. By what factor does $i_D$ increase?
steps.explanation:
Well into conduction $i_D \approx I_s e^{v_D/nV_T}$, so the ratio of two currents depends only on the voltage difference:
$\frac{i_{D2}}{i_{D1}} = \exp\left(\frac{\Delta v_D}{nV_T}\right) = \exp\left(\frac{ {{dV}} }{ {{n}}\times0.026 }\right)$ = {{f}}.

steps.prompt: A diode with $I_s = {{a}}\times10^{-14}$ A is reverse biased at $v_D$ = −{{VR|V}}, well below its breakdown voltage. What is $i_D$?
steps.explanation: $\exp(-{{VR}}/0.026)$ is practically zero, so $i_D = I_s(0 - 1) = -I_s = -{{a}}\times10^{-14}$ A. The minus sign means this tiny current flows from cathode to anode. A large reverse current only appears in breakdown.

steps.prompt: At $v_D$ = 0.6 V and 300 K ($n = 1$), the −1 in the Shockley equation changes $i_D$ noticeably.
steps.explanation: $\exp(0.6/0.026) = \exp(23.1) \approx 10^{10}$. Subtracting 1 from $10^{10}$ is negligible, so in forward conduction $i_D \approx I_s e^{v_D/nV_T}$.

steps.prompt: Find the thermal voltage $V_T = kT/q$ at a junction temperature of {{T}} K. ($k = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K, $q = 1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)
steps.explanation: $V_T = \frac{kT}{q} = \frac{1.38\times10^{-23}\times {{T}} }{1.60\times10^{-19}}$ = {{VT|V}}. Compare: about 26 mV at 300 K.

steps.prompt: Match each quantity with its typical value
steps.explanation: The saturation current is extremely small, which is why a forward voltage of 0.6–0.7 V is needed before a useful current flows. $V_T = kT/q \approx$ 26 mV at room temperature, and $n$ lies between 1 and 2.

steps.prompt: A diode with $n$ = {{n}} has $v_D$ = {{v1|V}} at $i_D$ = {{i1|A}}. Find $v_D$ when $i_D$ = {{k*i1|A}}. Both points are well into forward conduction; $V_T$ = 26 mV.
steps.explanation:
Dividing the Shockley equations for the two points gives $i_{D2}/i_{D1} = \exp\left((v_{D2}-v_{D1})/nV_T\right)$, so
$v_{D2} = v_{D1} + nV_T\ln\frac{i_{D2}}{i_{D1}} = {{v1}} + {{n}}\times0.026\times\ln({{k}})$ = {{v2|V}}.
$I_s$ is not needed.

steps.prompt: Measurements at 300 K: raising $i_D$ tenfold (from 0.1 mA to 1 mA) increases $v_D$ by {{dv|V}}. Find the emission coefficient $n$.
steps.explanation:
For a tenfold current step, $\Delta v_D = nV_T\ln 10$. So
$n = \frac{\Delta v_D}{V_T\ln 10} = \frac{ {{dv}} }{0.026\times2.303}$ = {{n}}.

steps.prompt: A diode used as a thermometer is biased at a constant current. At 300 K, $v_D$ = {{v0|V}}. Using the typical temperature coefficient of −2 mV/K, estimate $v_D$ at {{T}} K.
steps.explanation:
At constant current the forward voltage changes by about −2 mV per kelvin:
$v_D \approx {{v0}} - 0.002\times({{T}} - 300)$ = {{v|V}}.
Higher temperature means lower voltage.

steps.prompt: Diodes A and B are connected in parallel, so they have the same $v_D$, and both are well forward biased. Both have $n = 1$, but $I_s$ of B is {{m}} times that of A. How do their currents compare?
options: B carries {{m}} times the current of A
B carries 1/{{m}} of the current of A
B carries $e^{ {{m}} }$ times the current of A
steps.explanation: With the same $v_D$, $i_D \approx I_s e^{v_D/nV_T}$ has the same exponential factor for both diodes. The currents are therefore in the ratio of the saturation currents: B carries {{m}} times as much.

steps.prompt: A diode with $n$ = {{n}} conducts well at 300 K. By how much must $v_D$ increase to multiply $i_D$ by {{k}}?
steps.explanation: $\Delta v_D = nV_T\ln\frac{i_{D2}}{i_{D1}} = {{n}}\times0.026\times\ln({{k}})$ = {{dv|V}}. A small voltage change gives a large current change: this is why a conducting diode is often modeled as a constant voltage.

steps.prompt: A diode with $I_s = {{a}}\times10^{-14}$ A and $n = 1$ carries $i_D$ = {{iD|A}} at 300 K. How much power does it dissipate?
steps.explanation:
First the voltage: $v_D = nV_T\ln(i_D/I_s + 1) = 0.026\ln\left(\frac{ {{iD}} }{ {{a}}\times10^{-14} } + 1\right)$ = {{vD|V}}.
Then $P = v_D i_D$ = {{vD}} V × {{iD|A}} = {{P|W}}.

steps.prompt: If the temperature rises while the current through a forward-biased diode is held constant, $v_D$ increases.
steps.explanation: Although $V_T$ increases with temperature, $I_s$ increases much faster. The net result is that the forward voltage at a fixed current **decreases**, by about 2 mV/K.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the $i_D$–$v_D$ characteristic of a diode (the tiny reverse current $-I_s$ is too small to see). In which region does the diode operate at point P?
steps.explanation:
Look at the signs of $v_D$ and $i_D$ and at the shape of the curve at P:
- **Forward bias:** $v_D > 0$ and a large positive current, on the steep rise above about 0.6 V.
- **Reverse bias:** $-V_{BR} < v_D < 0$; the curve lies flat on the axis because only $-I_s$ flows.
- **Breakdown:** $v_D \approx -V_{BR}$ with a large negative current: the steep drop on the left.
Here P is at $v_D$ ≈ {{px||2}} V.

steps.prompt: Read the breakdown voltage $V_{BR}$ of this diode from its characteristic. Give it as a positive number.
steps.hint: Find the negative voltage where the reverse current suddenly becomes large.
steps.explanation: In reverse bias the curve stays flat at $i_D \approx 0$ until $v_D$ reaches about {{-VBR|V}}; there it drops almost vertically because the diode breaks down. So $V_{BR}$ ≈ {{VBR|V}}. In breakdown the voltage stays close to $-V_{BR}$ whatever the current: zener diodes are built to use exactly this.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the forward characteristic of a small silicon diode. Read the diode voltage $v_D$ at which $i_D$ = {{I0|A}}.
steps.explanation: Follow the dashed line at {{I0|A}} until it meets the curve, then go straight down to the $v_D$ axis: $v_D$ ≈ {{vD||2}} V. Below about 0.5 V the current is invisible on this scale; above the knee a few tens of millivolts change the current a lot. That is why a conducting diode is often modelled as a fixed drop of about 0.7 V.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows the characteristic of a silicon diode? Every graph has $v_D$ on the horizontal axis and $i_D$ on the vertical axis, crossing at the origin, with the same scales.
steps.explanation: A diode conducts in one direction only: practically no current for negative $v_D$ and for small positive $v_D$, then a steep exponential rise at about 0.6–0.7 V. A straight line through the origin is a resistor (Ohm's law). A curve with a large current at **negative** $v_D$ is a diode connected the other way round, and a curve that conducts both ways behaves like two antiparallel diodes.

steps.prompt: Curves A and B show the same silicon diode measured at 25 °C and at 75 °C. Which curve was measured at 75 °C?
options: Neither: temperature does not move the characteristic
steps.explanation: At a fixed current the forward voltage of a silicon diode drops by about 2 mV per kelvin. Being 50 K warmer means about 0.1 V less for the same current, so the hot curve is the one shifted to the **left**: it reaches any given current at a lower voltage.

steps.prompt: On a **logarithmic** current axis the forward characteristic is a straight line: every tenfold increase of current needs the same voltage step $nV_T\ln 10$. The marked points are at {{v1||3}} V (100 µA) and {{v2||3}} V (10 mA). Find the emission coefficient $n$ ($V_T$ = 26 mV).
steps.explanation: From 100 µA to 10 mA the current rises by two decades while $v_D$ rises by {{v2-v1|V}}, so one decade takes {{(v2-v1)/2|V}}. Setting this equal to $nV_T\ln 10$: $n$ = {{(v2-v1)/2||3}} V / (0.026 V · 2.303) = {{n||2}}.
